videoTitle: Bleeding on Birth Control Doesn't Mean You're Pregnant. Here's Why.
videoDescription: Breakthrough bleeding is one of the most common side effects of hormonal birth control — but when you're also spiraling about pregnancy, it's hard to trust that. Here's what negative tests actually mean, when irregular bleeding needs follow-up, and why the anxiety loop is so real. Full breakdown linked in bio.
script: You're bleeding irregularly on birth control, tests are negative, and you're still convinced you might be pregnant. That spiral is exhausting — and it's not evidence.

Breakthrough bleeding happens because your uterine lining is adjusting to steadier hormone levels. It's especially common in the first few months, but missed pills, stress, and certain medications can trigger it later too.

A negative test means hCG is below 1. Standard tests turn positive around 25. If you're using condoms and birth control, your risk is already very low — a negative test on top of that is strong evidence.
The hook effect is real but extremely rare, usually only happening late in pregnancy when hCG is in the hundreds of thousands. If you're not experiencing other pregnancy symptoms, it's unlikely.
Heavy or prolonged bleeding should get checked — not because it's usually dangerous, but to rule out fibroids, polyps, or other causes. An ultrasound will give you a clear answer.
The most likely explanation is your body adjusting to hormones, not hidden pregnancy. The full breakdown on when to worry and what tests actually mean is linked.
